Chapter 1: Childhood in a World of Rules and Secrets
You know, some kids grow up surrounded by bedtime stories and backyard adventures. But for others—especially those born into the heart of a powerful organization—childhood looks and feels completely different. Their earliest memories? They’re shaped by rules, rituals, and this unspoken sense that the world beyond their walls is distant, maybe even a little dangerous.
In this kind of place, family bonds mean everything, but they’re always under pressure. Love and loyalty get tangled up, overshadowed by a cause that insists it’s bigger than any one person.
Imagine those early years. There’s this overwhelming feeling that you belong to something important. The adults around you? They’re always busy, their faces rarely breaking into smiles. There’s a steady buzz—meetings, drills, hushed talks in hallways. For a child, life feels safe, but it’s also tightly controlled, with every minute planned out. The organization’s language becomes your first language; its beliefs, your entire world.
Picture a young girl growing up like this. Her parents are admired, holding powerful roles, and their loyalty to the group is everything. She’s proud of them, sure, but she can’t help noticing how much responsibility weighs on their shoulders. There are moments of warmth—maybe a shared meal or a quiet chat—but they’re often cut short by urgent calls or the pull of duty. The message is clear as day: the group always comes first.
Even school is different here. There aren’t any traditional classrooms. Instead, kids are taught the organization’s lessons, focusing almost entirely on its teachings and practices. Curiosity about the outside? There’s just no room for it. And when a child does ask questions—especially those that might challenge the way things are—the answer is always the same: “This is how it must be.”
Friendships do bloom among the children, but even those are shadowed by a feeling of being watched. Trust is fragile. One day, your friend is right there, laughing and sharing secrets. The next, they might be gone—sent away, with no explanation. So, you learn fast: getting too close is risky, and the group’s loyalty always comes before your own feelings.
Discipline here is strict. Mistakes aren’t just corrected—they’re corrected in front of everyone, sometimes harshly. If you forget a rule or speak out of turn, you’re reminded, loud and clear, why obedience matters. After a while, you just want to please the adults. The fear of letting them down—or worse, being separated from your family—starts to shape everything you do.
Still, underneath it all, questions start to bubble up. Why are some things forbidden? Why do the grown-ups sometimes look so tired, so worried? Why is it dangerous to even talk about the outside world? Most of the time, you push those questions aside, but they never fully go away. They’re always lurking, waiting for a safe moment to come out.
As the years go by, that sense of isolation only grows. You’re told the outside world is scary—full of people who don’t understand or might even want to hurt you. The organization promises to keep you safe, but only if you follow every rule, no questions asked. For a child, that means living with this constant undercurrent of fear. Fear of making a mistake, of losing your family, of being cast out.
Yet, there are still bright spots. A shared joke, a quick game, the warmth of a parent’s hug. These small moments? They become lifelines—proof that love can survive, even in the most controlled environments. But that shadow, the one cast by the organization, never really goes away. It shapes every relationship, every hope, every single dream.
Growing up here means learning to hide your doubts, to quiet your curiosity, and to accept that your life isn’t really your own. The journey toward independence doesn’t start with open rebellion. It begins with a quiet, persistent feeling that something’s missing—a piece of yourself you just can’t find within the group’s boundaries.
